walkthroughs.body_html:
Philosophy of Religion: Philosophical Issues & Questions — a core area of A-Level Religious Studies.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Philosophy of Religion: Philosophical Issues & Questions brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Philosophy of Religion: Philosophical Issues & Questions.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: What is the problem of evil?
options: Aquinas's Five Ways are five Christian sacraments.
If God is all-loving, all-knowing and all-powerful, why does evil and suffering exist? Logically, all four cannot be true together without explanation.
It is the question of whether the devil really exists.
It is the question of whether evil people will go to hell.

mcqs.q: What does the secularisation thesis claim?
options: That as societies modernise, religion declines in social significance — though sociologists now debate this, since global religion has not declined uniformly.
Secularisation means everyone in modern countries is now atheist.
Secularisation means the separation of church and state.

mcqs.q: Hume argues that we cannot reason reliably about the cause of the universe because:
options: the universe is a unique effect, and causal inference depends on repeated experience of similar cases
the universe has no order to explain
causes always resemble their effects exactly
science has already identified the universe's cause

mcqs.q: F.R. Tennant's anthropic argument claims that:
options: the universe appears fitted to produce and sustain intelligent life, which is best explained by design
human beings are the physical centre of the cosmos
natural selection disproves any design
the universe must be eternal

mcqs.q: Kant rejected the ontological argument on the ground that:
options: existence is not a real predicate that can be included in a concept
God's existence is proved by practical reason alone
Anselm's definition of God is incoherent
the argument relies on sense experience

mcqs.q: The ontological argument is unique among the classical arguments because it is:
options: a priori and deductive, moving from the concept of God alone
based on observation of order in the world
an inductive argument from religious experience
dependent on the authority of scripture
